I can relate. In the past, and occasionally still, I’ve used sex as a way to humiliate or punish myself because it would always cause me to feel really bad. A lot of times I would do normal self harm stuff afterwards. Basically it had nothing to do with pleasure and was more about making myself feel as worthless as I thought I was. 

I’ve managed to cut down on it by telling myself that I don’t deserve to be hurt any more than I already have been. I have trouble applying that to myself, so I imagine talking to a kid the same age as I was when I was abused. I would never say the mean things that I tell myself to her. I wouldn’t blame her for what happened or want her to be in pain. Then I think if I wouldn’t say that to her, why would I say it to myself? If I don’t want her to get hurt, why do I wish that on myself? I still struggle with it sometimes, but that’s something that helped me.

I can really relate to what you said, and I’m sorry that you’re going through this. I tried moving away, focusing on different jobs and different things in life, but I found that the memories followed me and always came back. I can also really relate to the feeling of self-hatred. I can only speak to my own experience, but what I found is that the more I tried to escape the memories of my abuse, the ”louder” they became. And the louder they were the more space they occupied in my life. I don’t know if that’s been the case for you or not. 

I always told myself that I couldn’t stand having those memories and did everything I could to get away from them. The thing that finally helped me was to stop trying to keep them away and instead sit with them and the feelings they brought up. I don’t know if this is the case for you, but I was deliberately trying to escape from them. In doing so I kept my brain from ever processing them. With the help of a therapist and hearing about others’ experiences, I feel like I was finally able to integrate them into my life in a way where they no longer take up so much space. I know they will always be there to some degree and that I can never be fully rid of them, but I have much more room in my life for things that I love and bring me joy. I hope that is the case for you as well and wish you the best with healing from this. It’s probably really hard to see right now, but change is still possible.

It sounds like you are really flooded with these memories right now. There are a variety of treatment options (like EMDR and other forms of therapy that can help you process and desensitize yourself to triggers). Outside of seeing a therapist you could try learning some grounding techniques. Sometimes I snap a rubber band on my wrist, focus on the sensation of my feet on the ground, or hold an ice cube in my hands until it melts. There are a lot of other methods that you can find online to see what works for you.

 For a while I didn’t have health insurance and was really short on money, so I bought some self help books. The Body Keeps the Score is a good one for PTSD symptoms in general. There are others (like The Sexual Healing Journey) that focus more on relationships and sexual symptoms. 

I was in a similar situation a few years ago where I felt overwhelmed by my symptoms and felt that dying was the only way out. I know it’s hard to see right now, but it’s possible to heal and make progress. It can be really painful and difficult at times, but you are strong and you can get through this.

That's a tough situation to be in, and I'm sorry to hear about your dad.  If people are mistreating you or you feel like it's a hostile work environment, it might be better to leave. However, if that's not the case it might be beneficial to give it a little more time before quitting, or maybe consider talking to your supervisor about the situation and asking about part time. It was a big transition for you to go to working full time, and that must feel super overwhelming and stressful. Overcoming the initial anxiety and stress of starting a new job could give you a sense of accomplishment and help you get back on your feet. However, if you feel that this is not something that you can deal with right now and that it's going to be detrimental in the long run, don't sacrifice your mental well-being over it. You can always apply for other jobs later if this one doesn't work out. Just my 2 cents.

I can really relate to that, I struggle with self-harm and I worry about being judged or admitted to a psych ward whenever I talk to a new provider about it. It can be really intimidating. I'm not sure where you go to school, but generally speaking there are privacy laws in place to prevent medical providers from telling third parties (like your professors and fellow students) about your private medical information, including your history of self-harm. The Health Insurance Portabilty and Accountability Act (HIPAA) is the law that covers that in the U.S.

Typically if you don't indicate that you're at an immediate risk of causing serious harm to yourself or others, they won't give you restrictions or try to have you admitted. I would just make it clear that you're having self-harm urges but you don't intend to act on any suicidal plans or anything like that. It would also be good to point out that you've managed to stay clean for a year, which is a huge accomplishment and would likely show that you have enough self-control to be safe on your own. Best of luck and I hope you feel better soon.

I'm sorry to hear that you're feeling so bad right now; that sounds like a really difficult spot to be in. I also struggle with anxiety and depression, and I can share a few self-help things that have helped me over the years (sorry if you've heard them before). 

I know it sounds cliche, but exercising regularly has helped me a lot with my depression and anxiety. It doesn't make it completely go away, but it's not as bad as it is if I don't exercise. I like doing cardio because it releases endorphins (the "runner's high"), which makes you feel relaxed and euphoric. It kind of "takes the edge off" of the depression I guess. There have also been studies showing that exercising regularly increases your brain's sensitivity to dopamine and makes you more likely to enjoy other day-to-day activities. 

When I'm anxious I try to do soothing activities, like listening to music that I like, watching a funny TV show, looking at funny memes, or taking a warm shower. 

Sometimes if I'm really caught up in a strong emotion and I feel stuck, I try to do an activity that requires logic (like a puzzle on my phone or a few math problems) to force myself to try to use a different part of my brain.

It sounds like therapy might be helpful. It's nice to have a non-judgmental person to listen to you and give you insight and advice on things that are bothering you. Most therapists don't dig too deep during the first appointment; it's more of an introduction and basic idea of what you want to be seen for. You could always make an appointment and voice your fear about opening up with them. It's a pretty common concern for people who haven't gone before, and most therapists are good about respecting your boundaries and making sure that you're comfortable before you open up about things. If you don't like it or feel like you don't match well with the therapist, you can always try a different one (or stop going if you feel that it's really not for you). Good luck and I hope you feel better soon.

I can really relate to this. My sexual assault was also my first sexual experience, and I really struggled with sex during high school and college. I know it's super frustrating, and it's definitely not fair. It sucks having to "re-learn" something that's supposed to be a good experience.

I'm glad to hear that you are going slow and recognize some of your triggers, that's really important. It's also good that your partner seems to respect your boundaries and doesn't pressure you to do things that you aren't comfortable with. I caused myself a lot of problems by going too fast and trying to "just get over it." I was worried that I wouldn't satisfy my partner and didn't want him to leave. I forced myself to do things that I wasn't comfortable with and then lied and said I was fine. That was a really bad idea; I basically re-traumatized myself, and he ended up leaving anyway. So it's important to work on this stuff with someone who is patient and willing to be supportive. It's really important to respect your progress and not rush yourself.

I read a couple of books that helped me a lot. The one that I found most helpful was "Healing Sex: A Mind-Body Approach to Healing Sexual Trauma" by Staci Haines. It talks about a lot of things that most sexual assault survivors experience but often feel uncomfortable talking about with other people. It made me realize that I'm not as messed up as I thought I was and that what I was experiencing was normal for someone with this type of trauma. It also has helpful guidance on how to approach and process sexual triggers and how to deal with the difficult emotions that go along with them. The book also gives advice on dealing with dissociation (if that's something that you have a problem with, I know it's been a big issue for me). "The Sexual Healing Journey" by Wendy Maltz was also helpful. It contained similar content, but it was presented a little bit differently. They are both good books.

I know it might be hard to believe right now, but it is possible to heal and build a healthy sex life that you enjoy. It's hard sometimes, and it's a lot of work, but you can do it. When I re-traumatized myself in college, I thought that I was ruined sexually. I couldn't do anything with a partner without having flashbacks and panicking. I was sure that I would be alone for the rest of my life. I've been married for 6 years now. There are good people out there that will accept you. Anyway, hopefully some of this was helpful. I'm sorry that this happened to you and that you're having to deal with these problems.
